h1: What to write on the back of a beer can and what to leave off
title: Back of Can Copy: What to Write | Craft Beer School
desc: How to plan the back panel of a beer can in India: the legal lines first, then the words that help a shopper pick your beer, then what to cut.
teaser: The front sells the can. The back closes the sale or loses it, usually in about four seconds.
standfirst: The back of a can carries the law, the facts a drinker needs and a few lines of brand voice, all on a curved strip the width of a thumb. Here is how we plan that strip so it works in a hot Indian store fridge.
sections: Start with what the law reserves

Before anyone writes a clever line, block out the space the regulations claim. Under FSSAI labelling rules for alcoholic beverages and your state's excise label approval, a beer pack in India carries the brand and product name, alcohol strength, net volume, the manufacturer or brewer details, the FSSAI logo and licence number, a batch or lot code, the date of manufacture, a best before date for most beers and the statutory health warning. Many states also want the MRP or a state-specific line. Some want the label registered with excise before sale.

The exact list changes with notifications and varies by state, so treat this as a checklist to confirm with your licensing consultant, not a final word. Our guide to beer label rules in India goes through it in more detail.

The practical point for a writer: on a 330 ml can these items can eat a third of the back panel. Measure them at real size first. Copy that gets written before the legal block is placed always ends up too long.

A person holding your can in a wine shop is asking what it tastes like, how strong it is and whether it is fresh. Answer those and the rest is decoration.

  • Taste. One sentence in plain words. "Bright and bitter, with grapefruit and pine" beats a paragraph about passion.
  • Strength and style. ABV is already on the pack by law. Put the style name near it so a reader can connect "6.5% IPA" without hunting.
  • Freshness. A packed-on date that a shopper can actually read matters more for an IPA than for a lager. Print it where the inkjet can reach and the fridge light can find it.

If you have space left, a food suggestion helps Indian shoppers more than a hop list. "Good with fried fish or a chicken 65" is a reason to buy tonight.

Most back panels open with a story paragraph. Few people read it in a shop. A single line in the brand's voice works harder: something a person might repeat to a friend. Write ten versions, read them aloud, keep the one that sounds like the people who run the brewery.

Keep the story for places where people have time: the website, the taproom menu, a QR code that opens a page about the beer. The can is a sign, not a brochure.

Watch the advertising rules too. Copy that suggests beer improves performance, mood or social success is a risk in India and a poor look anywhere. So is anything aimed at younger drinkers.

• Long hop and malt lists. Brewers love them. Shoppers skim past them. Name one or two if they mean something to your drinkers.
  • IBU without context. A number like 60 means little to most buyers. "Properly bitter" says the same thing to more people.
  • Awards you cannot show. If you mention a medal, name the competition and year so it can be checked.
  • Health or calorie claims. Leave them off entirely unless your adviser has cleared the exact wording.
  • Every social handle. One QR code or one handle is enough.

A can curves away from the eye, so only a narrow vertical strip reads at once. Keep body copy in a column rather than across the full width. Use a size the regulations accept as a floor, then go bigger where you can. Thin light type on a dark metallic finish disappears under fridge LEDs.

One floor detail worth knowing: cans in Indian cold chains often sweat when they come out of a fridge into 35 °C air. Condensation on a matt varnish or paper label blurs small type and smears a cheap inkjet code. Test your back panel by chilling a printed sample and leaving it on a shop counter for ten minutes.
A working order for the back panel

1. Place the legal block at true size and confirm it with your consultant.
  2. Reserve the batch code and date area where the coder can reach it.
  3. Write the taste sentence and the style line.
  4. Add one brand line and one food suggestion if space allows.
  5. Add a single QR code or handle.
  6. Print a sample, chill it, read it at arm's length under shop lighting.

The order matters because each step takes space from the next. Teams that start at step three end up shrinking the legal text, which is the one thing they cannot do.

This guide covers the words. Fitting them onto a pack with the right print process, finish and cost per unit is a bigger job. It is where most first launches stumble.
faqs: Do I need to print the health warning in a regional language?
Some states have asked for label text in the local language as well as English. Check your state's current excise notification or ask a licensing consultant before you print.
Should I put tasting notes or a story on the back?
Tasting notes, in one plain sentence. Put the longer story on your website or behind a QR code where people have time to read it.
Where should the batch code go?
Wherever your filling line's coder can print it cleanly, usually the base or a clear area near the seam. Agree the spot with the canning team before the artwork is final.
